newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE-Saudi poised to unearth more natural riches.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Saudi poised to unearth more natural riches.

text.p: Saudi Arabia has ambitious plans to dig beneath its vast desert sands. But this time it will be searching for minerals rather than oil to boost its wealth.

The world's richest oil producer already mines eight tonnes of gold a year, but its wealth of zinc, copper, bauxite, phospates, silver, iron and yet more gold are waiting to be exploited as part of a drive to reduce reliance on oil earnings of $40 billion yearly.

Analysts say slow government approval for exploration licences is holding back development of the sector, which is forecast to grow faster than any other in the state's five-year plan to 2000, at an average annual real rate of nine percent.
"The new minister is pushing hard to develop the industry, but the Saudi government has to move faster to develop the minerals sector," said one Saudi executive.

"The main mining ventures are taking so much time because the mining industry is pretty new so there is plenty of red tape," said another mining executive, of the numerous projects which have been on the drawing board for years.
They include four gold and silver deposits, which like other Saudi sites are likely to be developed as open-pit mines.

"Because they lack previous experience in these fields it is pretty natural that a mining licence should take longer than one for oil. But these have taken far too much time," he said, adding some firms had waited for over three years for a licence.
The government plan for the economy up to the year 2000 concedes that this discourages foreign private involvement, so far limited to Swedish firm Boliden Mineral Aktiebolag, a unit of Trelleborg.

"The main reasons preventing the private sector engaging in mining activities are: the long procedures involved in obtaining mining concessions, the fact that many promising mining deposits are often located in remote areas, and inadequate financial support..." the state plan says.

A Saudi firm, Arabian Shield Development Co which is listed in the United States, has a mining concession for the al-Masane deposit in the southwest, but production is not due to start until late 1997.
The government is taking steps to improve things. It is setting up a state-owned firm -- the Saudi Arabian Mining Co, Maadin -- which analysts say will be given some independence.
"This is a positive move and part of plans to diversify away from oil," said a Western diplomat in Riyadh.

"Now the ministry is looking at changing its approach on processing quotations to make it similar to (state oil firm Saudi) Aramco. The new arrangement will be set up in the new year. It might speed up procedures," said a mining executive.
Aramco, the world's largest oil firm, has administrative and structural freedoms which few state firms enjoy in the kingdom.
The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources has also set up a committee to reassess previous mining practice and look at ways to encourage private investment of the sector.
Executives said incentives for foreign investors include a five-year tax holiday and exemption from duty on main imports.

But these have not been enough to lure private firms. "One important change would be if they ease the mining code to make it easier for foreign companies to seek and get mining licences. That is paramount if the sector is to prosper," said one.

The state plan to 2000 speaks of eventual private sector involvement: "In the longer term, when the profitability of Petromin's precious metals activities becomes more firmly established, shares in Petromin's minerals company will be offered to private investors."
Apart from private participation, executives also see a need for development of supporting infrastructure around reserves, which are widely scattered across the huge desert kingdom.
Despite offers to develop a phosphate deposit in the north, analysts say the estimated $1.7 billion project is unlikely to come on stream before 2000 because of its inaccessibility.

"The directorate general of mineral resources is meeting firms in November to look at bids for the al-Jalamid phosphate mine. But by the time the bids are accepted and construction starts, production is unlikely for another five or six years because it is so remote," said the Western diplomat.
"First they have to decide how they will get phosphates to customers and ports," he added.
